title: The Four Inches Behind a Stranger's Eyes
book: Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind
author: Al Ries and Jack Trout
wiifm: HomeownersLoan and Apply4Loan compete in a market crowded with brokers who all say roughly the same thing. This is the book that explains why sounding the same is fatal, and what to do about it. You will follow two admen, Al Ries and Jack Trout, from the advertising department of General Electric to a partnership that gave every marketing meeting its vocabulary. You will learn their big ideas, the ladder in the mind, being first, owning one word, and also where hard data has since shown them to be wrong.

b: Al Ries was born in Indianapolis in 1926. After university at DePauw in Indiana he went into advertising and ended up working in the advertising department of General Electric, then one of the great training grounds of American marketing. In the early nineteen-sixties he left to start his own agency in New York.

Jack Trout was born in Queens, New York, in 1935, and he too passed through General Electric's advertising department. In the late nineteen-sixties he joined Ries's agency, and the two men began a partnership that would last a quarter of a century.

Neither of them was a famous creative talent. Their genius was for diagnosis. They watched campaigns that were beautifully made fail completely, and campaigns that looked crude succeed, and they asked why. Their answer would turn upside down the way marketing thought about itself.

General Electric taught them something by accident. It was a vast company that made almost everything, from light bulbs to jet engines, and its name stood for a general idea of electrical competence rather than for any one thing. Ries and Trout would later use companies like it as warnings. A name that means everything, they argued, ends up meaning nothing very sharp in a customer's head.
ch.cap: Ries and Trout study a company that makes everything

b: In 1969 Trout published an article in the trade magazine Industrial Marketing using a word that would define their careers: positioning. In 1972 the pair wrote a series of articles for Advertising Age called The Positioning Era Cometh, and the idea spread through the industry. In 1981 they expanded it into the book we are following, Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind.
Their central claim fits into one sentence from the book. Positioning is not what you do to a product. It is what you do to the mind of the prospect.

That was a startling shift. For a century marketers had assumed the battle was in the factory, the product or the advert. Ries and Trout said the battle was in a small, crowded, defensive human memory that had better things to do, and that most contests were already decided there before you opened your mouth.

The timing mattered. The nineteen-sixties had been the age of the creative revolution, when agencies like Doyle Dane Bernbach made witty, beautiful advertising and won prizes for it. Ries and Trout argued that cleverness was no longer enough. In a world filling up with products and messages, the question was not how brilliant your advert was, but whether there was any room left in the customer's head for what it said.
ch.cap: The word 'positioning' slips out into the industry

b: Their starting point was written before the internet and has only become truer since. We live, they said, in an overcommunicated society. Far more messages arrive than any mind can handle, so the mind does not handle them. It defends itself. It rejects anything that does not fit what it already knows, and accepts at most a simple label it can file next to labels it already holds.

The consequence is brutal. Your prospect is not carefully comparing you with your rivals. They have given you one word, or no word, quickly and on thin evidence, and they will not revise it, because revising it would take effort they have no reason to spend.

So the task is not to describe yourself accurately. It is to find a word you can plausibly own, and then own it, without wavering, for years. Their advice was that in an overcommunicated society the best strategy is the oversimplified message.

They had an image for what this does to the customer. The mind, they said, is like a sponge that is already full. You cannot pour more in without squeezing something out. So the one strategy that rarely works is the one most companies try first: telling the customer a lot of new information about themselves. The ones that work begin with what is already in the mind and connect to it.
ch.cap: Messages pour in; the full-sponge mind keeps one word

b: The story Ries and Trout loved best was not theirs. In 1962 the car rental firm Avis had lost money for more than a decade and was being beaten soundly by Hertz. It hired the agency Doyle Dane Bernbach, where a copywriter named Paula Green wrote a line that said what no company ever says aloud: when you're only number two, you try harder. It became simply, we try harder.
Within a year, by the usual account, Avis had moved from a loss of about three million dollars to a profit of over one million. The line ran for fifty years before Avis retired it in 2012.

For Ries and Trout, the genius was not the humility. Everyone already knew Hertz was bigger, and Avis could not shift that belief. So instead of fighting it, Avis claimed it. It agreed with what was already in the customer's mind and, in doing so, became the only other rental company anyone could name. Be careful with the legend, though. The often-quoted market share figures have grown in the retelling, which is rather the point of the book.
ch.cap: Avis, only number two, tries harder at the counter

b: Their most useful picture is the ladder. Imagine that for every product category the mind holds a small ladder, with one brand on each rung. Most ladders have only a few rungs, often just two, and the ladder is longer for things you care about.

Two things follow. Getting onto a full ladder means knocking someone off, and memory does not do that as a favour. But you can choose your ladder. If you cannot win a rung on the big one, build a new category where the top rung is empty and climb that instead.

Hence their advice about attacking a market leader head-on: don't. The leader's place in memory is what makes it easy to think of and therefore easy to buy. Shouting that you are better than the leader just reminds everyone of the leader. Avis did not claim to be better than Hertz. It claimed the second rung outright.

Try it on your own business. Ask ten customers, separately, to finish the sentence: you are the one that. Do not prompt or explain. If you get ten different answers, you have no position, only ten private theories, and the next competitor to say one clear thing will take the rung. If you get the same answer nine times and you do not like it, the problem is not your wording. You are trying to hold a rung that someone else owns, and you need a different ladder.
ch.cap: Ladders in the mind; a newcomer climbs an empty one

b: If the ladders are full, where do you go? Ries and Trout borrowed a French phrase for the answer: cherchez le créneau, look for the hole. Instead of asking what the company is good at, ask what space in the customer's mind is still empty. It might be a size, a price, a type of customer or a particular moment of need that no brand has yet claimed.

Their favourite example was the Volkswagen Beetle. When it arrived in America, the market believed cars should be long, low and glamorous. Doyle Dane Bernbach's famous campaign told Americans to think small. Instead of pretending the Beetle was a proper big car, it claimed the hole that was sitting in plain sight, the small car, and turned its smallness into the whole point.

The book is equally fierce about names. A name, they argued, is the first point of contact between a message and a mind, and a good one should begin the positioning process by telling the customer what the product is for. They warned against what they called the no-name trap: companies that shrink to strings of initials and assume customers will remember what the letters stand for. Initials work, they said, only for companies that were already famous under their full name.

And they turned the same thinking on people. In a chapter on positioning yourself and your career, they advised finding a horse to ride: a company, a boss, an idea or a cause that is going somewhere, because nobody gets far on their own legs alone. It is a typically unsentimental piece of advice, and it fits the rest of the book. Even a person, in a crowded world, is filed under one word.
ch.cap: Among long glamorous cars, a Beetle claims the hole

b: Their most quoted device goes like this. Everyone knows Charles Lindbergh was the first to fly the Atlantic alone, in 1927. Who was second? Their answer was Bert Hinkler, a better pilot, they said, and nobody remembers him. The mind stores a category under whoever got there first and throws the rest away.

Here is the delicious correction. The example is wrong. Hinkler's solo crossing, in 1931, was of the South Atlantic. The second solo crossing of the North Atlantic is usually credited to Amelia Earhart in 1932, and she is someone everybody remembers. A book about how the mind clings to tidy, simplified facts rested on a tidy, simplified fact. The punchiest slogans, like it is better to be first than to be better, belong to their later book of 1993, The 22 Immutable Laws of Marketing.

The bigger claim has actually been tested. In 1993 the researchers Peter Golder and Gerard Tellis studied around five hundred brands in fifty categories using historical records. Almost half of the pioneers had failed. Only about one in nine still led the category it created. The companies that came later and led the market did much better. Ries and Trout's reply was that failed pioneers were first in the market but never first in the mind. That makes their law impossible to disprove. Keep the insight, which is real: the mind favours whoever got there first. Drop the idea that it is a law.
ch.cap: Lindbergh first, 1927; the second flyer was Earhart

b: If every rung is taken and you cannot build a new ladder, there is one more move. You can change what customers believe about the brand standing where you want to be. Ries and Trout called this repositioning the competition.

Their textbook case was Tylenol, which did not claim to be better than aspirin. It ran advertising about what aspirin could do to some people, such as stomach irritation and bleeding, and spoke to those who should not be taking it. The customer had to defend their own body, not a brand.

The other great case was 7-Up. In 1968 its agency launched the Uncola, with psychedelic posters and the actor Geoffrey Holder's huge laugh on television. It did not attack Coke or Pepsi. It split the shelf into cola and not-cola, and made 7-Up the leader of the second.

Here is the ending they do not give you. Through the nineteen-seventies Sprite, backed by Coca-Cola's enormous distribution, steadily ate into 7-Up's share. A position in someone's mind turns out to be rented, not owned, and the rent is paid in being easy to buy.

The lesson for a small firm is uncomfortable. A clever idea about where you sit in the customer's mind is worth a great deal, but it does not protect you from a rival who is simply everywhere. A broker whose name is sharp but who cannot be found at the moment a homeowner searches is a brand nobody can buy. The position has to be paired with presence.
ch.cap: 7-Up splits the shelf: cola and the Uncola

b: The idea that made Ries famous, and later a little obsessive, was the line-extension trap. Your brand name is the hook that hangs you on a rung, and it works because it means one thing. Every time you stretch it over a neighbouring product, you ask the customer's memory to hold two meanings under one name. Memory, being lazy, holds neither clearly.

Managers love line extensions because they are cheap and bring in revenue this year. Ries argued they borrow from an account nobody keeps: the clarity of the name, spent bit by bit until the brand stands for a general area and a focused rival takes the rung.

This is where the book is most overstated. Studies of packaged goods have found that most line extensions do reasonably well and can even strengthen the parent brand. Diet Coke, one of the biggest extensions in history, is a standing rebuttal. The fair verdict is that the danger Ries spotted is real and underestimated by managers, but he stated it as a law on the evidence of anecdotes.

The practical test is simple. Before you add the neighbouring service because three customers asked for it, write down the single word you currently own and ask whether it survives. Then ask whether the new thing could launch under a different name. If that would make it much harder to sell, the new product is borrowing trust from the old one rather than building its own, which is exactly the transaction Ries was warning about.
ch.cap: One name stretched over everything frays and sags

b: In 1994 the partnership ended. Trout set up his own firm and Ries worked with his daughter Laura. Trout died in 2017 and Ries in 2022, aged ninety-five. Between them they had given marketing the words it still uses, often without knowing where they came from.

The strongest challenge to their ideas came from the data. In 2010 Byron Sharp of the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute published How Brands Grow, drawing on decades of real buying records. Brands, he found, grow mainly by getting more people to buy them, not by deepening loyalty. Customers of rival brands see them in almost the same way, so most claimed differences are invisible to buyers. What matters is being easy to think of at the moment of buying and easy to buy. And the useful kind of difference is distinctiveness: colours, logos and sounds that make you recognisable, not arguments that make you special.

So here is the fair reading. Ries and Trout were right about where the battle is fought: in memory. They saw it decades before the data. They were wrong about how it is won. They thought you won by narrowing to one idea and defending it. The evidence says you win by being recognisable and easy to reach, for as many people as possible, as often as possible. Their insight survives. The spreadsheet changes the advice.
ch.cap: Partners split; buying records reveal how brands grow

take: The battle is in the mind
Customers file you under one word, fast, and rarely revise it. Decide what word you want to own before you spend another pound on ads.
Ask customers to finish the sentence
Ask ten customers to finish: you are the one that... If you get ten different answers, you have no position yet.
Agree with what they already believe
Avis won by admitting it was number two. If the market already knows something about you, use it rather than fight it.
If the top rung is taken, find a narrower category where it is empty, such as a specific kind of homeowner or a specific situation, and lead that.
Most market pioneers failed or lost the lead. Speed matters less than staying easy to find and easy to buy.
Stretching one brand over too many services blurs what it means. Before adding a new line, ask whether it could launch under a different name.
Buyers rarely notice claimed differences. Consistent colours, logos and phrases that make you instantly recognisable do more work.
7-Up's clever Uncola lost to Sprite's distribution. Keep paying the rent by being visible wherever and whenever customers are ready to act.
recall: What is the ladder model, and what two conclusions follow?

The mind holds a small ranked ladder for each category, one brand per rung. Getting onto a full ladder means displacing someone, which memory resists. So you can choose a different ladder, a narrower category where the top rung is empty.
Why was the Avis campaign so effective?

Everyone already believed Hertz was bigger, and Avis could not change that. By claiming the number two spot openly, Avis agreed with what customers already believed. That made it the only other rental company people could name.
What was wrong with the Hinkler example?

Hinkler's 1931 solo flight crossed the South Atlantic, not the North. The second solo North Atlantic crossing is usually credited to Amelia Earhart in 1932, who is famous. The book's example of a forgotten second-comer is itself a convenient simplification.
What did Golder and Tellis find about pioneers?

Studying about five hundred brands in fifty categories, they found nearly half of pioneers failed and only about one in nine still led their category. Later entrants that became leaders did much better. Ries and Trout answered that failed pioneers were never first in the mind, which makes the claim unfalsifiable.
How does Byron Sharp's evidence challenge positioning?

His buying data show brands grow mainly by gaining more buyers, not loyalty, and that customers barely notice claimed differences. What matters is being easy to think of and easy to buy, and being distinctive rather than differentiated. The battle is in memory, but it is won differently.
note: Documented: Trout's 1969 Industrial Marketing article, the 1972 Advertising Age series, the 1981 book, the 1993 22 Immutable Laws, the 1994 split, and the deaths of Trout in 2017 and Ries in 2022. The Avis campaign of 1962 and its retirement in 2012 are well recorded, though the often quoted market share figures are inflated. The Hinkler example is historically wrong, as noted. Golder and Tellis (1993) and Sharp (2010) are the main empirical challenges; the source dated Ries's own agency to 1961, but most accounts give 1963, so it is described here only as the early 1960s.
words: The person or organisation currently holding a position, such as a market leader.
Ries and Trout warned against attacking the incumbent head on, because shouting that you are better than the leader only reminds people of the leader.
The quality of standing out and coming readily to mind.
Byron Sharp's data suggests brands win through salience, being easy to think of at the moment of buying, more than through a narrow claimed difference.
Framed in such a way that no possible evidence could ever prove it wrong.
When failed pioneers were explained away as first in the market but not first in the mind, the law of being first became unfalsifiable.
Based on individual stories or examples rather than systematic evidence.
Ries stated the line-extension trap as a law, but his evidence was anecdotal, and studies later found most extensions do reasonably well.
The weakening of something by spreading it too thinly or mixing it with other things.
The line-extension trap is a warning about dilution: stretch a brand name over too many products and it stops meaning anything sharp.
stories: In 1962 the car rental firm Avis had lost money for more than a decade and was being beaten soundly by Hertz. Its agency, Doyle Dane Bernbach, did something no company ever does: it admitted it was losing. The copywriter Paula Green wrote that when you're only number two, you try harder, and it became simply, we try harder. Within a year, by the usual account, Avis had gone from a loss of about three million dollars to a profit of over one million, and the line ran for fifty years. Avis could not shift the belief that Hertz was bigger, so it claimed second place and owned it.

Ries and Trout loved this party trick. Everyone knows Charles Lindbergh was the first to fly the Atlantic alone, in 1927. Who was second? Nobody remembers, they said. It was Bert Hinkler, a better pilot, forgotten because the mind keeps whoever got there first and throws the rest away. Lovely point, wrong fact. Hinkler's solo flight in 1931 crossed the South Atlantic. The second solo crossing of the North Atlantic is usually credited to Amelia Earhart, in 1932, and she is one of the most famous aviators who ever lived. A book about how minds cling to tidy facts rested on a tidy fact.
The Uncola, and the rival that ate it

By the late nineteen-sixties Coca-Cola and Pepsi owned the soft-drinks ladder. So in 1968 the agency behind 7-Up launched the Uncola, with psychedelic posters and the actor Geoffrey Holder's enormous laugh on television. It did not attack the colas. It split the shelf in the customer's mind into cola and not-cola, and made 7-Up the leader of the second. Ries and Trout held it up as textbook repositioning. Here is the ending they leave out. Through the nineteen-seventies Sprite, backed by Coca-Cola's vast distribution, steadily ate into 7-Up's share. A position in the mind turns out to be rented, not owned, and the rent is paid in being easy to buy.
biz: Ask ten recent HomeownersLoan customers, separately and without prompting, to finish the sentence: you are the one that. Write down the answers word for word. Ten different answers means you have no position yet. If one answer keeps coming back, and it is true and compliant, build around it: ad headlines, the homepage and the first WhatsApp message, held steady for years. Then pair it with presence, because a sharp name nobody can find at the moment of searching cannot be bought. Ask Grok to report branded search volume and impression share monthly as your measure of the position taking hold.

Ries warned that stretching one name over a neighbouring product leaves the customer holding two meanings and trusting neither. For Ruby Holdings there is a sharper reason. Debt Support Direct should mean one thing, help for people struggling with debt, and it must never become a route to sell secured loans. Offering more borrowing to a client in financial distress under the same name would blur the brand and raise serious Consumer Duty and conflict-of-interest concerns. This week, check every Debt Support Direct page, email footer and WhatsApp template for loan wording or links, and keep the loan brands entirely separate.
connects: Ries and Trout's advice never to attack the market leader head on is Liddell Hart's indirect approach moved from the battlefield into the customer's mind.
Building a new ladder where the top rung is empty is Thiel's argument for creating a category you can own instead of fighting in a crowded one.
The overcommunicated mind that files each brand under one quick label is Kahneman's lazy, fast System One at work.
recap:
Al Ries and Jack Trout were not famous creative talents. They were two advertising men who had both passed through General Electric, and their gift was diagnosis. They watched beautiful campaigns fail and crude ones succeed, and they asked why. In nineteen sixty-nine Trout gave the answer a name, positioning, and in nineteen eighty-one the pair set it out in this book.

Their central claim turned marketing inside out. Positioning is not what you do to a product. It is what you do to the mind of the prospect. The battle is not fought in the factory or the advert. It is fought in a small, crowded, defensive memory that has better things to do.

We live, they said, in an overcommunicated society. The mind is a sponge that is already full. It rejects whatever does not fit what it knows and files each brand under one word, quickly and for good. So the best strategy is the oversimplified message.

Picture a ladder in the mind for every category, with a brand on each rung and often only two rungs. Do not attack the leader head on, because shouting about the leader only reminds people of it. Avis did the opposite. It admitted it was number two, promised to try harder, and kept that line for fifty years. If every rung is full, look for the hole, as the Volkswagen Beetle did when it told Americans to think small. Or reposition the competition, as 7-Up did when it became the Uncola. And beware the line-extension trap, stretching one name over so many things that it means none of them.

Now the honest part. Their famous example of the forgotten second pilot across the Atlantic was simply wrong, and the second person was Amelia Earhart, whom everyone remembers. Research on hundreds of brands found that most pioneers do not end up leading. And in two thousand and ten, Byron Sharp's buying data showed that brands grow mainly by being easy to think of and easy to buy for as many people as possible, not by defending one narrow idea. Even the Uncola was slowly eaten by Sprite, which was simply everywhere.

So keep the insight and update the advice. Ries and Trout were right about where the battle is fought, in memory, decades before the data proved it. They were less right about how it is won.

The line to remember is theirs, with one amendment. Own a place in the mind, then make sure you are always within reach.
